akiec.name: Actinic Keratosis
akiec.description: A rough, scaly patch of skin caused by years of sun exposure. It is considered a precancerous lesion, meaning it can potentially develop into skin cancer (most often squamous cell carcinoma) if left untreated.
characteristics: Rough, dry, or scaly texture
Pink, red, or brownish color
Usually on sun-exposed areas (face, ears, scalp, hands, forearms)
Often easier to feel than to see
warning_signs: Lesion becomes thicker or raised
Becomes tender, itchy, or starts bleeding
Rapid growth in size
Ulceration or a sore that does not heal
general_care: Protect the area from further sun exposure (sunscreen, protective clothing)
Avoid picking or scratching the lesion
Do not attempt to treat or remove it yourself
akiec.professional_advice: Because actinic keratosis is precancerous, a dermatologist should evaluate and, if needed, treat this lesion. Early treatment is simple and highly effective.

bcc.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
bcc.description: The most common form of skin cancer. It usually grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body, but it can damage surrounding skin and tissue if left untreated.
characteristics: Pearly or waxy bump, sometimes with visible blood vessels
Flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion
A sore that repeatedly heals and reopens
Most common on sun-exposed skin (face, neck, ears)
warning_signs: A sore that bleeds, oozes, or crusts and does not heal within a few weeks
Visible growth or change in size or shape
New shiny or pearly bump on the skin
general_care: Avoid sun exposure and use sun protection
Do not delay seeking a professional opinion
Keep the area clean and avoid irritating it
bcc.professional_advice: This pattern is associated with skin cancer. Prompt evaluation by a dermatologist is strongly recommended — basal cell carcinoma is highly treatable when caught early.

bkl.name: Benign Keratosis
bkl.description: A general category of non-cancerous skin growths (such as seborrheic keratoses or solar lentigines) caused by a buildup of skin cells. These are extremely common, especially with age, and are not dangerous.
characteristics: Waxy, "stuck-on" appearance
Light brown to black in color
Well-defined borders
Usually stable in size and shape over time
warning_signs: Sudden change in color, size, or shape
New irregular or asymmetric borders developing
Bleeding, itching, or pain without an obvious cause (e.g. friction)
general_care: Generally no treatment is needed
Monitor for any changes over time
Avoid scratching or picking at the lesion
bkl.professional_advice: Benign keratoses are typically harmless. Still, if this lesion changes in any way, have it checked by a dermatologist to rule out other conditions that can look similar.

df.name: Dermatofibroma
df.description: A common, benign, firm nodule that forms in the skin, often on the legs. It is thought to form as a reaction to a minor injury such as an insect bite and is not cancerous.
characteristics: Small, firm bump under the skin
Brown, pink, or reddish color
Dimples inward when pinched from the sides
Usually stable and painless
warning_signs: Rapid growth in size
Change in color or shape
Becomes painful, itchy, or starts bleeding on its own
general_care: Usually requires no treatment
Avoid unnecessary irritation or picking
Monitor for any changes over time
df.professional_advice: Dermatofibromas are benign. If it changes noticeably or bothers you, a dermatologist can confirm the diagnosis and discuss removal options.

mel.name: Melanoma
mel.description: The most serious form of skin cancer, developing in the pigment-producing cells (melanocytes). It can spread to other parts of the body if not caught early, which makes prompt evaluation important.
characteristics: Often follows the ABCDE pattern: Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Color, large Diameter, Evolving over time
May appear as a new mole or a change in an existing mole
Can occur anywhere on the body, not only sun-exposed areas
warning_signs: Asymmetrical shape or irregular, blurred borders
Multiple colors or uneven color distribution within the lesion
Diameter larger than a pencil eraser (~6mm)
Any change in size, shape, color, or elevation
Bleeding, itching, or crusting
general_care: Do not attempt self-treatment or removal
Avoid further sun exposure to the area
Take a photo to track any changes until you are seen
mel.professional_advice: This AI prediction should not be considered a diagnosis, but because melanoma can be serious, prompt professional dermatological evaluation is strongly recommended. Please consult a qualified dermatologist as soon as possible.

nv.name: Melanocytic Nevus
nv.description: Commonly known as a mole. It is usually a benign growth of pigment-producing cells (melanocytes) and is extremely common — most adults have several.
characteristics: Usually well-defined and symmetric
Even color throughout (tan, brown, or black)
Often stable in size and shape over months to years
Can be flat or slightly raised
warning_signs: Rapid change in size
Change in color or an uneven color pattern developing
Irregular or blurred borders appearing
Bleeding, itching, or a new lesion that looks unusual
general_care: Monitor the mole for changes over time (consider periodic photos)
Protect skin from excessive UV exposure
Seek medical advice if the lesion changes
nv.professional_advice: Most moles are harmless and need no treatment. If you notice any of the warning signs above, have it examined by a dermatologist to be safe.

vasc.name: Vascular Lesion
vasc.description: A growth made up of blood vessels, such as a cherry angioma, hemangioma, or similar. These are common and almost always benign.
characteristics: Red, purple, or blue in color
Often small, round, and dome-shaped
May blanch (lighten) briefly when pressed
Usually stable over time
warning_signs: Rapid growth in size or number
Persistent bleeding or a lesion that does not stop bleeding easily
Sudden change in color or shape
Pain or ulceration
general_care: Usually no treatment needed
Avoid trauma to the area (they can bleed if scraped)
Monitor for any changes over time
vasc.professional_advice: Vascular lesions are typically benign. If it bleeds persistently, grows quickly, or changes noticeably, have it evaluated by a dermatologist.
